questions.stem: In a GP consultation, Linh says: "Jasper has had this cough every day for five weeks and nothing is working." Jasper is 2 years 4 months old. Amoxicillin, prednisolone liquid and a salbutamol puffer with a spacer have all failed. Which history question is most likely to uncover a cause that earlier clinics missed?
options: "Is the cough worse at night, with cold air, or when Jasper runs around or laughs?"
"Does anyone in the family have asthma, eczema or hay fever?"
"How did the cough start? Any choking or gagging while eating or playing?"
"Has Jasper been near anyone with tuberculosis, or travelled overseas?"
questions.why: Inhaled foreign body peaks at 1 to 3 years. The choking episode is often brief, and parents may forget it or not mention it, so you must ask directly about a sudden start and any choking or gagging (here, on mixed nuts) in any toddler whose cough has not responded to treatment.
notes: Triggers like night, cold air and exercise point to asthma, which was already treated and did not respond; asking about them will not find a missed cause.
Asking about atopy and family history helps judge asthma risk, but asthma has already been treated without effect, and this question would not reveal the choking event.
TB is worth asking about when there is lobar collapse, but it is far less likely in a well toddler with no contact or travel, and it is not the cause most often missed here.

questions.stem: Jasper, 2 years 4 months, choked on mixed nuts at a party 5 weeks ago and has coughed ever since. On the right he has reduced air entry, a dull base and a monophonic wheeze. The CXR shows right lower lobe collapse with volume loss. RR 44, SpO2 96% in room air, afebrile. What is the most appropriate next step from general practice?
options: Phone the paediatric team today for rigid bronchoscopy; keep Jasper nil by mouth
Book an outpatient CT chest and review Jasper with the result next week
Start amoxicillin–clavulanate for pneumonia and review in 48 hours
Arrange inspiratory and expiratory films, and refer only if air trapping is seen
questions.why: A suspected inhaled foreign body needs same-day referral to a paediatric centre for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia, which both confirms and removes it. Keep the child fasted for the anaesthetic, and call 000 if there is stridor, distress or falling SpO2.
notes: Waiting a week is unsafe, because the nut can move and block a larger airway. Even if CT were done, he would still need bronchoscopy to remove it.
This is a mechanical obstruction, so antibiotics will not fix it. He has already failed amoxicillin, and more antibiotics only delay diagnosis and raise the risk of bronchiectasis.
Normal extra films do not exclude a foreign body, and this history with focal signs already justifies bronchoscopy, so making referral depend on more imaging delays care.

questions.stem: Jasper's CXR shows a triangular opacity at the right lung base. The trachea and mediastinum are shifted to the right, the right hilum is lowered, and there are no air bronchograms and no effusion. He choked on nuts 5 weeks ago. What mechanism best explains this X-ray pattern?
options: Fluid in the right pleural space compressing the lower lobe
Ball-valve obstruction trapping air in the lobe beyond the nut during each expiration
Inflammatory exudate filling the alveoli while lobe volume is kept
Complete bronchial block, with the trapped gas absorbed into capillary blood
questions.why: When a bronchus is completely blocked, the gas beyond it keeps diffusing into pulmonary capillary blood, whose total gas pressure is below atmospheric, so the lobe deflates (absorption atelectasis). The resulting volume loss pulls the trachea, mediastinum and hilum towards the collapsed side.
notes: An effusion takes up space and pushes the mediastinum away from it, and the report says there is no effusion.
A ball-valve obstruction lets air in but not out, causing hyperinflation and a shift away from the affected side, which is the opposite of this film.
Consolidation keeps the lobe's volume, so there is no shift, and it usually shows air bronchograms. Neither fits this film.

questions.stem: Jasper's frontal CXR shows a triangular opacity at the right base, medially and behind the heart. The outline of the medial right hemidiaphragm is lost but the right heart border is preserved. Which lobe has collapsed, and on what anatomical basis?
options: Right middle lobe, as it lies against the right heart border
Right lower lobe, as it lies posteriorly on the diaphragm behind the heart
Right upper lobe, as it collapses down towards the right hilum
Right middle and lower lobes together, as both lie below the oblique fissure
questions.why: Silhouette sign: when the hemidiaphragm outline is lost but the right heart border stays sharp, the disease is in the lower lobe, which sits posteriorly on the diaphragm. The middle lobe lies against the right atrium, so middle lobe disease blurs the right heart border.
notes: Middle lobe collapse would blur the right heart border, which is preserved here, and it would not usually hide the medial hemidiaphragm.
Upper lobe collapse causes an opacity at the top of the lung and lifts the hilum, but this hilum is lowered and the opacity is at the base.
If the middle lobe were also collapsed, the right heart border would be lost as well, but here it is preserved.
